message.content:
A **CPU (Central Processing Unit)** and a **GPU (Graphics Processing Unit)** are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of tasks:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Primary Purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles a wide variety of tasks (OS, applications, etc.) | Specialized for parallel processing – originally for rendering graphics, now also used for many compute‑intensive workloads |
| **Core Count** | Few cores (typically 2–32) optimized for single‑thread performance | Hundreds or thousands of smaller cores optimized for executing many threads simultaneously |
| **Clock Speed** | Higher clock speeds (often > 3 GHz) because each core does complex work | Lower clock speeds (often < 1 GHz) because each core is simpler |
| **Architecture** | Complex control logic, large caches, branch prediction, out‑of‑order execution | Simpler, highly parallel architecture with many ALUs, less sophisticated control logic |
| **Memory Hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, high bandwidth memory access | Smaller per‑core caches; relies on shared memory pools and high‑bandwidth memory (e.g., GDDR6) |
| **Instruction Set** | Rich instruction set (x86, ARM, etc.) with many features for general computing | Often a subset of the CPU’s instruction set, focused on vector operations |
| **Typical Workloads** | Single‑threaded or lightly threaded tasks (web browsing, office apps, OS services) | Highly parallel tasks (graphics rendering, machine learning inference/training, scientific simulations) |
| **Energy Efficiency** | Optimized for power efficiency per core when doing complex tasks | Optimized for throughput per watt when running many simple operations in parallel |

### Why the Difference Matters

- **Parallelism**: GPUs can run thousands of lightweight threads at once, making them ideal for tasks that can be broken into many independent sub‑tasks (e.g., matrix multiplication). CPUs excel at tasks that require deep branching, complex decision trees, or low latency.
- **Flexibility**: CPUs can handle almost any software task because of their general‑purpose design. GPUs are more specialized but have become increasingly programmable (CUDA, OpenCL), allowing them to accelerate non‑graphics workloads.
- **Performance**: For pure graphics rendering, GPUs far outperform CPUs. For tasks that need heavy branching or sequential logic, CPUs still win.

In short, CPUs are like a Swiss Army knife—good at many things but not super fast at any one thing. GPUs are like a specialized tool kit—super fast at a narrow set of tasks that can be parallelized.
